```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)

n_users <- 4000
n_impression <- 100
target_baseline <- 0.935
ate_true <- 0.01049
sd_user <- 0.5

user_effect <- rnorm(n_users, mean = 0, sd = sd_user)

# Find the intercept that gives these 4,000 users a mean completion probability of 93.5%
alpha <- uniroot(
  \(alpha) mean(plogis(alpha + user_effect)) - target_baseline,
  interval = c(0, 10)
)$root

p_pre <- plogis(alpha + user_effect)

# Find the logit-scale effect that gives this finite sample an ATE of +1.049 pp
tau_logit <- uniroot(
  \(tau) mean(plogis(alpha + user_effect + tau) - p_pre) - ate_true,
  interval = c(0, 1)
)$root

p_post_0 <- p_pre
p_post_1 <- plogis(alpha + user_effect + tau_logit)
treated <- sample(c(
  rep(FALSE, n_users / 2),
  rep(TRUE, n_users / 2)
))

experiment <- tibble(
  user_id = seq_len(n_users),
  treated,
  pre_complete = rbinom(n_users, n_impression, p_pre),
  post_complete = rbinom(
    n_users,
    n_impression,
    if_else(treated, p_post_1, p_post_0)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    x = pre_complete / n_impression,
    y = post_complete / n_impression
  )

theta <- with(experiment, cov(y, x) / var(x))
x_bar <- with(experiment, mean(x))

experiment <- experiment |>
  mutate(
    y_cuped = y - theta * (x - x_bar),
    y_theta1 = y - (x - x_bar)
  )

estimate_diff <- function(data, outcome, method) {
  by_arm <- data |>
    summarise(
      outcome_mean = mean({{ outcome }}),
      variance = var({{ outcome }}),
      n = n(),
      .by = treated
    )

  estimate <- with(
    by_arm,
    outcome_mean[treated] - outcome_mean[!treated]
  )
  se <- with(by_arm, sqrt(sum(variance / n)))

  tibble(
    method,
    estimate,
    se,
    lower = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * se,
    upper = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * se
  )
}

estimates <- bind_rows(
  estimate_diff(experiment, y, "Difference in means"),
  estimate_diff(experiment, y_cuped, "CUPED (estimated theta)"),
  estimate_diff(experiment, y_theta1, "DiD (theta = 1)")
)

rho <- with(experiment, cor(x, y))
theta1_variance_ratio <- with(experiment, var(y_theta1) / var(y))
se_reduction <- with(
  estimates,
  1 -
    se[method == "CUPED (estimated theta)"] /
      se[method == "Difference in means"]
)
```

Up to the [previous article](/posts/causal-impact-bsts/), we estimated the effect of an ad-pause feature released only on iOS using difference-in-differences (DiD), the synthetic control method (SCM), and CausalImpact.

But there has been a catch in this example from the start.
Ad pause is a UI feature.
Before release, we could randomly split iOS users into two groups, enable the feature for only one group, and run an A/B test.
There would be no need to construct a counterfactual from Android or other devices.

Of course, running an experiment does not make every part of the analysis easy.
Here, the completion rate is already high, and the expected improvement is only about one percentage point (pp hereafter).
The variance of the estimate therefore matters.
Even with proper randomization, a wide confidence interval can obscure a small effect.

CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) addresses this problem by using pre-experiment data to reduce the variance of a randomized comparison.
In this article, we redesign the same ad-pause feature as a user-level experiment and examine how CUPED improves estimation precision.

## Experimental design with randomized comparison

The experimental unit is an iOS user.
Eligible users are randomly assigned 1:1.
The treatment group receives the ad-pause feature, while the control group keeps the existing UI.
Assignment remains fixed throughout the experiment.

The outcome $Y_i$ is each user's completion rate during the experiment: completed ad views divided by impressions.
Let $Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1)$ denote user $i$'s potential outcomes without and with treatment, and let $Z_i \in \{0,1\}$ denote assignment.
The estimand is the average treatment effect (ATE).

$$
  \tau = \mathbb{E}\left[ Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \right]
$$

For each user, we observe only the potential outcome corresponding to the assigned condition.

$$
  Y_i = Z_iY_i(1) + (1 - Z_i)Y_i(0)
$$

Even so, the difference in group means,

$$
  \hat{\tau}_{\text{diff}} = \bar{Y}_{Z=1} - \bar{Y}_{Z=0},
$$

estimates the ATE.
Randomization makes $Z_i$ independent of the potential outcomes, so the iOS users in the control group provide the comparison for what would have happened at the same time without the feature.
We no longer need to infer the counterfactual from observational data.
This removes the need for the parallel-trends assumption in DiD, the assumption in SCM that the factor structure remains stable after treatment, and the assumption in CausalImpact that the model structure remains stable.

Still, the word "randomized" alone does not guarantee a valid experiment.
At minimum, the implementation and logs must verify the following:

- Assignment remains fixed throughout the experiment, and no user appears in both groups.
- The treatment does not spill over to the control group.
- Users are not excluded from the analysis based on behavior observed after assignment.

As in the [first article in this series](/posts/causal-synthetic-data-design/), we simplify the setting by assuming that the ad-pause feature does not affect the number of impressions.
In practice, pausing may keep users watching and increase their subsequent impressions.
If so, impressions should be examined as a separate outcome alongside the completion rate.

## Estimation error after randomization

Randomization guarantees that, across repeated experiments, the expected difference in group means equals the true ATE.
It does not make the treatment and control groups identical in any one experiment.
If users who almost always watch ads to completion happen to be overrepresented in the treatment group, its completion rate will be higher even when the feature has no effect.
A larger sample reduces such chance imbalances, but both the experimental duration and the number of eligible users are limited.

This is where the pre-experiment completion rate becomes useful.
Users who usually have a high completion rate are likely to remain high during the experiment.
When the two measures are correlated, the pre-experiment outcome can remove some of the pre-existing variation between users and reduce the variance of the estimate.

## Variance reduction with CUPED

Let $Y$ be the completion rate during the experiment and $X$ the same outcome measured before the experiment.
Substantively, $X$ is a lagged outcome; in CUPED, it is used as a pre-treatment covariate.
Here, $X$ is calculated over a pre-experiment window of the same length as the experiment, and the outcome is adjusted as follows:

$$
  Y_{\text{adj}} = Y - \theta(X - \bar{X})
$$

Because $X$ is determined before treatment, it cannot be affected by treatment.
Here, $\bar{X}$ is the pre-experiment mean across all users, so $X - \bar{X}$ measures how far each user's pre-experiment outcome lies from that mean.
The adjustment lowers $Y$ for users with an above-average $X$ and raises it for users with a below-average $X$, removing variation that was already present before the experiment.

Applying the adjustment to both groups gives the following ATE estimator:

$$
  \hat{\tau}_{\text{CUPED}} = (\bar{Y}_1 - \theta\bar{X}_1)
                              - (\bar{Y}_0 - \theta\bar{X}_0)
$$

The adjusted outcome can also be written as $Y_{\mathrm{adj}} = Y - \theta X + \theta\bar{X}$.
The final term, $\theta\bar{X}$, is common to every user and therefore cancels when we take the difference between group means.
Under randomization, the expected pre-experiment difference $\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_0$ is zero.
Holding $\theta$ fixed, the adjustment therefore leaves the expected ATE unchanged.

The remaining question is how much to subtract, as determined by $\theta$.
CUPED, introduced to online experiments by [Deng et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2433396.2433413), uses the value that minimizes the variance of the adjusted outcome.
Expanding the variance gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
    \mathrm{Var}(Y_{\text{adj}})
     & = \mathrm{Var}(Y - \theta X)                \\
     & = \mathrm{Var}(Y) + \theta^2\mathrm{Var}(X)
    -2\theta\mathrm{Cov}(Y,X).
  \end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating with respect to $\theta$ gives the optimal coefficient:

$$
  \theta^* = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(Y,X)}{\mathrm{Var}(X)}.
$$

Writing the correlation between $X$ and $Y$ as $\rho$, the adjusted variance becomes

$$
  \mathrm{Var}(Y_{\text{adj}}) = \mathrm{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2).
$$

The stronger the correlation between pre-experiment and in-experiment completion rates, the greater the variance reduction from CUPED.
For example, if $\rho = 0.6$, the variance falls to $1 - 0.6^2 = 0.64$ of its original value.
The sample size required for the same power likewise falls to roughly 64%.
Conversely, CUPED offers little improvement when the correlation is weak because, for example, the pre-experiment window is short or the metric fluctuates substantially from day to day.

The population value $\theta^*$ is unknown, so in practice we estimate it from the covariance and variance in the experimental data.
Here, we estimate $\theta$ using the treatment and control groups together.

## Evaluation with synthetic user-level data

The device-by-day panel used so far does not contain user IDs, so it cannot provide user-level pre-experiment outcomes.
We therefore generate a separate synthetic user-level dataset for an experiment on the same ad-pause feature.

We assign 4,000 users equally between treatment and control and give each user 100 impressions before and during the experiment.
Under this simplification, the mean of the user-level completion rates equals the completion rate calculated across all impressions.
In practice, users have different numbers of impressions.
The estimand must therefore be specified in advance: either an equally weighted mean of user-level rates or total completions divided by total impressions.

To represent persistent differences in users' propensity to complete an ad, we share a user-specific effect $u_i \sim N(0,0.5^2)$ across the pre-experiment and experimental periods.
The standard deviation of 0.5 is not estimated from real data; it is chosen to induce enough correlation to make the effect of CUPED visible.
Completion rates are generated as follows:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
    X_i                       & \sim \frac{1}{100}\mathrm{Binomial}(100,p_i^{(0)}),   \\
    Y_i                       & \sim \frac{1}{100}\mathrm{Binomial}(100,p_i^{(Z_i)}), \\
    \mathrm{logit}(p_i^{(0)}) & = \alpha + u_i,                                       \\
    \mathrm{logit}(p_i^{(1)}) & = \alpha + u_i + \tau_{\mathrm{logit}}.
  \end{aligned}
$$

The two externally specified inputs are the 93.5% baseline and the +1.049 pp ATE, chosen to match the [first article in this series](/posts/causal-synthetic-data-design/).
We first generate $u_i$ for all 4,000 users and solve for the intercept $\alpha$ that makes their mean completion probability 93.5%.
We then solve for $\tau_{\mathrm{logit}}$ so that the ATE among the same 4,000 users is +1.049 pp.
Thus, rather than being fixed directly, $\alpha$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{logit}}$ are determined by the generated user population and the two target values.

The binomial draws for the pre-experiment and experimental periods are independent, but both use the same $u_i$.
Users who tend to have a high completion rate therefore remain more likely to have a high rate during the experiment.
@tbl-simulation-diagnostics summarizes the target values used for generation and the resulting coefficients, correlation, and variance ratios.
The calculation column makes the source of each value explicit.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-simulation-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: >-
#|   Simulation targets and calculated quantities.
#| echo: false
#| message: false

tibble(
  item = c(
    "Target baseline",
    "Target ATE",
    "alpha",
    "tau_logit",
    "rho",
    "theta",
    "CUPED variance ratio",
    "Theta = 1 variance ratio",
    "CUPED standard error reduction"
  ),
  calculation = c(
    "Fixed simulation target",
    "Fixed simulation target",
    "`mean(plogis(alpha + user_effect)) = target_baseline`",
    "`mean(plogis(alpha + user_effect + tau_logit) - p_pre) = ate_true`",
    "`cor(x, y)`",
    "`cov(y, x) / var(x)`",
    "`1 - rho^2`",
    "`var(y_theta1) / var(y)`",
    "`1 - se_cuped / se_unadjusted`"
  ),
  value = c(
    scales::percent(target_baseline, accuracy = 0.1),
    scales::number(
      ate_true * 100,
      accuracy = 0.001,
      prefix = "+",
      suffix = " pp"
    ),
    scales::number(alpha, accuracy = 0.001),
    scales::number(tau_logit, accuracy = 0.001),
    scales::number(rho, accuracy = 0.001),
    scales::number(theta, accuracy = 0.001),
    scales::percent(1 - rho^2, accuracy = 0.1),
    scales::percent(theta1_variance_ratio, accuracy = 0.1),
    scales::percent(se_reduction, accuracy = 0.1)
  )
) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::fmt_markdown(columns = calculation) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    item = "Quantity",
    calculation = "Calculation",
    value = "Value"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_align(align = "right", columns = value) |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Lora"))
```

The CUPED variance ratio in @tbl-simulation-diagnostics is calculated from $1 - \rho^2$.
We next compare the unadjusted estimator, CUPED, and the adjustment with $\theta = 1$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-estimates
#| tbl-cap: >-
#|   ATE estimates from the randomized comparison (pp).
#|   The true value is +1.049 pp.
#| echo: false
#| message: false

estimates |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, se, lower, upper),
    decimals = 3,
    scale_by = 100
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    method = "Estimator",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    se = "Standard error",
    lower = "95% CI lower",
    upper = "95% CI upper"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_align(align = "right", columns = -method) |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Lora"))
```

All three estimates in @tbl-estimates are close to the true value.
The standard error is smaller under CUPED, with the reduction reported in @tbl-simulation-diagnostics.
Whether the point estimate happens to move closer to the truth in this single simulation depends on the random draw, but across repeated experiments the estimates vary less.
What matters for CUPED is not whether this particular point estimate is closer to the truth, but the difference in interval width.

```{r}
#| label: fig-estimates
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Point estimates and 95% CIs for the ATE.
#|   The vertical dashed line marks the true value of +1.049 pp.
#| echo: false

estimates |>
  mutate(method = fct_rev(method)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ate_true, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.15) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Average treatment effect", y = "Estimator") +
  theme_classic(base_family = "ubuntu", base_size = 13)
```

## The roles of DiD and CUPED

Revisiting the CUPED estimator reveals its relationship to DiD:

$$
  \hat{\tau}(\theta) = (\bar{Y}_1 - \theta\bar{X}_1)
                       - (\bar{Y}_0 - \theta\bar{X}_0).
$$

Setting $\theta = 1$ gives

$$
  \hat{\tau}(1) = (\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{X}_1) - (\bar{Y}_0 - \bar{X}_0),
$$

which is the same expression as DiD: calculate the pre-post change in each group and then take the difference between those changes.
This connection appears in [Ding's (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18793) treatment of covariate adjustment and [Courthoud's (2024)](https://matteocourthoud.github.io/post/cuped/) comparison of CUPED and DiD.
The algebra may be the same, but the two methods serve different purposes.

  |                                   | DiD with observational data                                    | CUPED in a randomized comparison                        |
  | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Basis for counterfactual          | Parallel-trends assumption                                     | Random assignment                                       |
  | Purpose of pre-period             | Remove time-invariant group differences to identify the effect | Remove chance pre-period differences to reduce variance |
  | Coefficient on pre-period outcome | Fixed at $\theta = 1$                                          | Estimate $\theta^*$ to minimize variance                |

In the [DiD article](/posts/causal-did-parallel-trends/), subtracting the change on Android from the change on iOS was itself the identification strategy used to remove time variation.
Here, iOS users are randomly split into two groups, so the effect is identified without subtracting the pre-experiment difference.
CUPED uses the pre-experiment outcome only to reduce the variance of the estimate.
This distinction also explains why fixing $\theta = 1$ does not always reduce variance.

$$
  \mathrm{Var}(Y - X) = \mathrm{Var}(Y) + \mathrm{Var}(X) - 2\mathrm{Cov}(Y,X).
$$

If $X$ and $Y$ both have variance $\sigma^2$, the right-hand side becomes $2\sigma^2(1 - \rho)$.
This is smaller than the unadjusted variance $\sigma^2$ only when $\rho > 0.5$.
Mechanically subtracting the pre-experiment outcome can therefore increase variance when the correlation is weak.

For $\theta = 1$, @tbl-simulation-diagnostics reports the ratio $\mathrm{Var}(Y - X)/\mathrm{Var}(Y)$.
It is below the unadjusted variance in this dataset, but it does not fall as far as under CUPED with the optimal $\theta$.
DiD fixes the coefficient at one for identification, whereas CUPED estimates the coefficient to minimize variance.
That difference is visible here.

## Implementation in BigQuery

CUPED does not require a machine-learning model.
It can be implemented by preparing each user's pre-experiment completion rate $X$, experimental outcome $Y$, and assignment $Z$, then calculating the mean and variance of $X$ and the covariance of $X$ and $Y$.

The SQL below follows the same simplification as the synthetic data: every user in the analysis has a completion rate in both the pre-experiment and experimental periods.
If real data do not satisfy this condition, users cannot be selected based on whether their experimental-period outcome is observed.
The analysis population and the treatment of zero-impression users must be specified before assignment.

Suppose `experiment_events` contains `user_id`, `arm`, `period`, `impression`, and `complete`.
We first calculate each user's completion rate in both periods, then calculate $\theta$ and the adjusted outcome.

```sql
WITH user_metrics AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    ANY_VALUE(arm) AS arm,
    SAFE_DIVIDE(
      SUM(IF(period = 'pre', complete, 0)),
      NULLIF(SUM(IF(period = 'pre', impression, 0)), 0)
    ) AS x,
    SAFE_DIVIDE(
      SUM(IF(period = 'post', complete, 0)),
      NULLIF(SUM(IF(period = 'post', impression, 0)), 0)
    ) AS y
  FROM `project.dataset.experiment_events`
  GROUP BY user_id
),

cuped_parameter AS (
  SELECT
    AVG(x) AS x_bar,
    SAFE_DIVIDE(COVAR_SAMP(y, x), VAR_SAMP(x)) AS theta
  FROM user_metrics
),

adjusted AS (
  SELECT
    arm,
    y,
    y - theta * (x - x_bar) AS y_cuped
  FROM user_metrics
  CROSS JOIN cuped_parameter
)

SELECT
  arm,
  COUNT(*) AS n_users,
  AVG(y) AS mean_unadjusted,
  AVG(y_cuped) AS mean_cuped,
  VAR_SAMP(y_cuped) AS var_cuped
FROM adjusted
GROUP BY arm
;
```

This query returns the mean and variance for each arm.
The difference in `mean_cuped` between treatment and control is the CUPED estimate of the ATE.
Its standard error can be calculated by dividing each arm's `var_cuped` by its user count and summing the results.

When implementing CUPED, the following data-quality checks matter more than whether the SQL happens to run:

- `arm` is unique within each user.
- The pre-experiment window closes before assignment.
- The analysis population is not selected using events observed after assignment.
- A single person is not represented by separate IDs on different devices and assigned to both treatment and control.

The final check is particularly important for multi-device services.
If the same person appears under different IDs in both arms, spillover and assignment contamination follow.

## Counterfactuals and experimental design

Across this series, we have evaluated the same ad-pause feature in several ways.

  | Method                | Construction of the counterfactual                              | Main cost or limitation                                               |
  | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Pre-post comparison   | Use pre-treatment iOS directly                                  | Cannot separate time variation from the treatment effect              |
  | DiD                   | Remove time variation using the change on Android               | Parallel-trends assumption                                            |
  | SCM                   | Reproduce pre-treatment iOS with a convex combination of donors | Continued factor structure; coarse rank-based inference               |
  | CausalImpact          | Predict post-treatment iOS with a model                         | Dependence on the model, priors, and structural stability             |
  | Randomized comparison | Assign contemporaneous iOS users to control                     | Experimental implementation, sample size, and operational constraints |

Observational methods are necessary when evaluating an intervention after the fact because an experiment was not possible.
But an intervention that can be randomized, such as a UI feature, need not be turned into an observational problem from the outset.
Randomization places a comparison group that supports the counterfactual inside the experiment itself.

CUPED improves estimation precision without changing that experimental design.
Causal identification comes from random assignment, not from CUPED.
The first question should therefore be whether the comparison group can be built into the design.
Only when that is difficult should methods such as DiD, SCM, or CausalImpact be used to construct the counterfactual.

## R code

```r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)

n_users <- 4000
n_impression <- 100
target_baseline <- 0.935
ate_true <- 0.01049
sd_user <- 0.5

user_effect <- rnorm(n_users, mean = 0, sd = sd_user)

# Find the intercept that gives these 4,000 users a mean completion probability of 93.5%
alpha <- uniroot(
  \(alpha) mean(plogis(alpha + user_effect)) - target_baseline,
  interval = c(0, 10)
)$root

p_pre <- plogis(alpha + user_effect)

# Find the logit-scale effect that gives this finite sample an ATE of +1.049 pp
tau_logit <- uniroot(
  \(tau) mean(plogis(alpha + user_effect + tau) - p_pre) - ate_true,
  interval = c(0, 1)
)$root

p_post_0 <- p_pre
p_post_1 <- plogis(alpha + user_effect + tau_logit)
treated <- sample(c(
  rep(FALSE, n_users / 2),
  rep(TRUE, n_users / 2)
))

experiment <- tibble(
  user_id = seq_len(n_users),
  treated,
  pre_complete = rbinom(n_users, n_impression, p_pre),
  post_complete = rbinom(
    n_users,
    n_impression,
    if_else(treated, p_post_1, p_post_0)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    x = pre_complete / n_impression,
    y = post_complete / n_impression
  )

theta <- with(experiment, cov(y, x) / var(x))
x_bar <- with(experiment, mean(x))

experiment <- experiment |>
  mutate(
    y_cuped = y - theta * (x - x_bar),
    y_theta1 = y - (x - x_bar)
  )

estimate_diff <- function(data, outcome, method) {
  by_arm <- data |>
    summarise(
      outcome_mean = mean({{ outcome }}),
      variance = var({{ outcome }}),
      n = n(),
      .by = treated
    )

  estimate <- with(
    by_arm,
    outcome_mean[treated] - outcome_mean[!treated]
  )
  se <- with(by_arm, sqrt(sum(variance / n)))

  tibble(
    method,
    estimate,
    se,
    lower = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * se,
    upper = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * se
  )
}

estimates <- bind_rows(
  estimate_diff(experiment, y, "Difference in means"),
  estimate_diff(experiment, y_cuped, "CUPED (estimated theta)"),
  estimate_diff(experiment, y_theta1, "DiD (theta = 1)")
)

# Simulation targets and calculated quantities
rho <- with(experiment, cor(x, y))
theta1_variance_ratio <- with(experiment, var(y_theta1) / var(y))
se_reduction <- with(
  estimates,
  1 -
    se[method == "CUPED (estimated theta)"] /
      se[method == "Difference in means"]
)

tibble(
  target_baseline,
  target_ate = ate_true,
  alpha,
  tau_logit,
  rho,
  theta,
  cuped_variance_ratio = 1 - rho^2,
  theta1_variance_ratio,
  se_reduction
)
```
